subject: lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite;

messages.author: b52f6f335543f6ce
messages.subject: lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite;
parts:
Hi everybody,

I'm new to the lavaan package and I'm trying to perform a CFA on my sample of 15114 observations and 24 variables, it's a likert scale.
I'm not trying to validate a psychometric tool, but rather to look at its psychometric properties and to conclude if it's adapted or not to use on our sample.

Here's my model :
mod_base <-
  "
Physique =~ K_K_1_1_b + K_K_1_2_b + K_K_1_3_b + K_K_1_4
Emotion =~ K_K_2_1 + K_K_2_2_b + K_K_2_3_b + K_K_2_4_b
Estime =~ K_K_3_1 + K_K_3_2 + K_K_3_3 + K_K_3_4
Famille =~ K_K_4_1 + K_K_4_2 + K_K_4_3_b + K_K_4_4_b
Ami =~ K_K_5_1 + K_K_5_2 + K_K_5_3 + K_K_5_4_b
Ecole =~ K_K_6_1 + K_K_6_2 + K_K_6_3_b + K_K_6_4_b
"

I obtain the following warning message :
Warning message:
In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables
                is not positive definite;
                use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv") to investigate.

I ran some investigations and detected negative values in the determinants and in the eigenvalues. Since the size of the sample is not so small, maybe the problem may come from there (so I would conclude it's a variance problem) or our data is not well adapted, meaning that this psychometric tool is not adapted for our data - or both. Would you agree with my conclusions? Do you have other hypotheses and tests that I could run? Is there anything that I could do or just conclude that we can't use this tool for our sample?

 Here are the results of the investigations and also the complete output of the model.
Thank you everybody in advance!

messages.subject: Re: lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite;
parts:
Hi,

See this article for an excellent explanation of NPD in correlation matrices in the context of latent variable modelling and potential solutions:

Urbano Lorenzo-Seva & Pere J. Ferrando (2021) Not Positive Definite Correlation Matrices in Exploratory Item Factor Analysis: Causes, Consequences and a Proposed Solution, Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 28:1, 138-147, DOI:10.1080/10705511.2020.1735393

The negative eigenvalue in your output is the problem and shows you the source of NPD (and also why the determinant is negative). 

One solution is to take the correlation/covariance matrix and make it positive definite through some kind of bending algorithm. I am not a stats/quant expert, so take that piece of advice with a grain of salt / do some reading on correlation matrix bending in the context of latent variable models. There are a bunch of R packages that do this kind of bending, e.g.,

mbend
fungible
psych
correlation
Matrix

I like mbend and Matrix functions due to the range of options they allow and the in-depth output that I can inspect when making NPD matrices PD. But your mileage will vary between the various packages.

Hope this helps,

Ian

Hi everybody,

I'm new to the lavaan package and I'm trying to perform a CFA on my sample of 15114 observations and 24 variables, it's a likert scale.
I'm not trying to validate a psychometric tool, but rather to look at its psychometric properties and to conclude if it's adapted or not to use on our sample.

Here's my model :
mod_base <-
  "
Physique =~ K_K_1_1_b + K_K_1_2_b + K_K_1_3_b + K_K_1_4
Emotion =~ K_K_2_1 + K_K_2_2_b + K_K_2_3_b + K_K_2_4_b
Estime =~ K_K_3_1 + K_K_3_2 + K_K_3_3 + K_K_3_4
Famille =~ K_K_4_1 + K_K_4_2 + K_K_4_3_b + K_K_4_4_b
Ami =~ K_K_5_1 + K_K_5_2 + K_K_5_3 + K_K_5_4_b
Ecole =~ K_K_6_1 + K_K_6_2 + K_K_6_3_b + K_K_6_4_b
"

I obtain the following warning message :
Warning message:
In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables
                is not positive definite;
                use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv") to investigate.

I ran some investigations and detected negative values in the determinants and in the eigenvalues. Since the size of the sample is not so small, maybe the problem may come from there (so I would conclude it's a variance problem) or our data is not well adapted, meaning that this psychometric tool is not adapted for our data - or both. Would you agree with my conclusions? Do you have other hypotheses and tests that I could run? Is there anything that I could do or just conclude that we can't use this tool for our sample?

 Here are the results of the investigations and also the complete output of the model.

vnt...,
If you have reason to be very certain that your model is correct and the data is the problem, then forcing the model to estimate may be the best option.  However, if it seems plausible that the model could be an over-simplification, then it might be a good idea to first examine the item correlation matrix, implied correlation matrix, residual correlation matrix, and perhaps modification indices to locate the points of stress in the model.  I do not see obvious red flags in your estimates but what does stand out is the standardized covariance of .9 between the first two factors and what seem like relatively large standardized unique variances.  Whether these are problematic may depend on your test design and construct theory.

Once you have a feel for where the problems are, you might try building up the model in steps.  Fit each one-factor model separately.  Then add factors one at a time.  It might be informative to begin with the factors that show the most sign of problems to see those problems in isolation before working your way up to the full model.  It could be that you need some correlated uniquenesses or cross loadings, but given your sample size (and that strong correlations between factors also increases statistical power), these may be required for fitting the model without having much practical implications for the test if the estimates are near zero.  With only four items per factor, you do not have much leeway for removing items.  So, modeling the quirks seems like the best strategy.

Keith
